findings.title: Recovery codes are written to user storage unhashed
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes to JSON and passes them directly to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...). The local-DB path goes through RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues, which keeps only hashed codes (verification hashes the input with hashRawCode). The user-storage path has no equivalent step, so plaintext recovery codes are persisted into external user storage (LDAP, custom federation, etc.). Anyone with read access to that store can take over accounts. The codes should be hashed the same way before being handed to user storage, and the storage-side verification adjusted to match.

findings.title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed and can be replayed
findings.body: isValid for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks membership in the stored list and never marks the used code as consumed or removes it. The authenticator's 'all codes used' logic (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator) works on the local credential model and calls removeStoredCredentialById, which does not touch federated credentials. So a recovery code that has been used can be used again indefinitely when the credential lives in user storage. The test added (testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin) only covers one successful login and never checks that a used code is rejected, so this gap is not caught.

findings.title: Javadoc typo in getCredential return description
findings.body: The @return text reads 'a optional  credential model' (grammar 'an optional' and a double space). Minor, but it is a public utility method's contract documentation.
